title: Verifying passwords safely
summary: Check a login against a stored hash with a constant-time comparison, upgrade old hashes, and meet bcrypt and Argon2.

steps.title: Checking a login
body: To verify a login you never "unhash" anything. You repeat the hashing with the **same** salt and settings, and compare:
```text
stored:  pbkdf2-sha256$600000$<salt>$<hash>
typed:   "correct horse"
1. split the stored string on '$'
2. read iterations and salt from it
3. compute Pbkdf2(typed, salt, iterations)
4. compare with the stored hash
If the user typed the right password, step 3 reproduces exactly the bytes in step 4.
The way you *compare* in step 4 matters more than you would think. That is the next card.

steps.explain: Split first, then read the three stored pieces (in any order), recompute, and compare last.

steps.title: Comparing without leaking time
body: The obvious comparison stops at the first byte that differs:
```csharp
for (int i = 0; i < a.Length; i++)
if (a[i] != b[i]) return false;   // returns early

So a guess that matches the first 10 bytes takes a little longer to reject than one that matches none. Measured over many requests, that difference tells an attacker how much of a secret they have right, one byte at a time. This is a **timing attack**, and it is practical against secrets compared over a network: API keys, HMAC signatures, session tokens, reset codes.
The fix is a comparison whose running time depends only on the length, never on the contents:
```csharp
bool same = CryptographicOperations.FixedTimeEquals(actual, expected);
It looks at every byte whatever happens. Use it **whenever you compare a secret or a MAC**. `SequenceEqual`, `==` on strings and `string.Equals` all exit early.

steps.explain: Equal contents give `True`. Different lengths return `False` straight away, which is fine: the length of a hash or MAC is not a secret.

steps.prompt: Which comparisons should use `CryptographicOperations.FixedTimeEquals`? Select all that apply.
options: A computed password hash against the stored hash
An HMAC signature on a token against the one you compute
An API key sent by a client against the stored key
A username typed at login against `"admin"`
steps.explain: Anything secret, or a MAC that proves knowledge of a secret, gets a constant-time comparison. A username is not secret.

steps.title: Upgrading hashes, and the other algorithms
body: Because the stored string records its own settings, you can raise the work factor without a migration:
```text
on successful login:
if stored iterations < current policy
rehash the password (you have it in plain text right now) and save the new string
Old hashes upgrade themselves as users log in. This is called **rehash on login**.
PBKDF2 is not the only choice. You will meet:
| Algorithm | Notes |

| **Argon2id** | Winner of the Password Hashing Competition (2015) and OWASP's first choice. **Memory-hard**: each guess needs a lot of RAM, which GPUs and custom chips are bad at. Tuned by memory, iterations and parallelism. |
| **bcrypt** | Since 1999, still solid. Cost factor is a power of two (`$2b$12$...` is 2^12 rounds). Only uses the first 72 bytes of a password. |
| **scrypt** | Also memory-hard. |
| **PBKDF2** | Built into .NET and FIPS-approved, which matters in regulated industries. Not memory-hard, so use a high iteration count. |
In .NET, PBKDF2 is in the box; Argon2 and bcrypt come from NuGet packages. ASP.NET Core Identity's `PasswordHasher` uses PBKDF2 with a format very like the one you are building.
> **Tip:** Never invent a scheme such as `SHA256(SHA256(pw) + pepper)`. Use one of these, with their recommended settings.

steps.prompt: Match each algorithm to what sets it apart.
pairs: cost is a power of two, reads only 72 bytes

steps.prompt: A stored hash says `pbkdf2-sha256$100000$...` and your policy is now 600,000. The user logs in with the correct password. What should happen?
options: Log them in, and replace the stored string with a new hash at 600,000 iterations
Reject the login until they reset their password
Log them in and leave the old hash forever
Decrypt the old hash and re-encrypt it with the new settings
steps.explain: At the moment of a successful login you hold the plain password, so you can rehash it with the current policy. There is nothing to decrypt.

steps.title: Verify and upgrade
prompt: Stored strings look like `pbkdf2-sha256$<iterations>$<salt base64>$<hash base64>` (the format from the last lesson).

- `bool Verify(string password, string stored)`: `true` only when the password produces the stored hash. Return `false` (never throw) when the string does not have exactly 4 parts or does not start with `pbkdf2-sha256`. Compare with `CryptographicOperations.FixedTimeEquals`.
- `bool NeedsRehash(string stored, int currentIterations)`: `true` when the stored iteration count is lower than `currentIterations`.
The tests also give you `HashPassword(password, salt, iterations)` from the last lesson, ready to use.
solution: byte[] actual = Rfc2898DeriveBytes.Pbkdf2(password, salt, iterations, HashAlgorithmName.SHA256, expected.Length);
hints: Split on `'$'`; check the part count and `parts[0]` before reading anything.
Derive with `expected.Length` as the output length, then `FixedTimeEquals(actual, expected)`.
`NeedsRehash` is one line: parse `parts[1]` and compare.
template: string HashPassword(string password, byte[] salt, int iterations) =>
Dojo.Eq("Verify accepts the right password", true, Verify("correct horse", dojoStored));
Dojo.Eq("Verify rejects a wrong password", false, Verify("correct h0rse", dojoStored));
Dojo.Eq("Verify rejects the empty password", false, Verify("", dojoStored));
Dojo.Eq("Verify accepts a known stored value", true, Verify("correct horse", "pbkdf2-sha256$1000$AAECAwQFBgcICQoLDA0ODw==$yRTMTwbMbo9G0VfjobWqerzuuxe7BETNTErBbKKumGQ="));
Dojo.Eq("Verify returns false for a malformed string", false, Verify("x", "garbage"));
Dojo.Eq("Verify returns false for another algorithm", false, Verify("x", "md5$1$AA==$AA=="));
